name: Rapamycin (sirolimus)

track.title: Lab & animal
track.line: Extended mouse lifespan, started late in life (2009)

track.title: Phase I
track.line: Phase 1/2 aging trials recruiting, e.g. NCT06727305

what.text: Sirolimus, also called rapamycin, is an mTOR inhibitor. mTOR is a protein that controls cell growth. Sirolimus is a prescription medicine that suppresses the immune system. Its label says it is used to prevent rejection of a transplanted kidney and to treat a rare lung disease called lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM).
In mice, rapamycin added to food from about 600 days of age extended median and maximum lifespan in both sexes, at three test sites. That study is the main reason rapamycin is discussed for aging.
Sirolimus is FDA approved for transplant and some rare diseases. Using it for longevity is off-label. No trial has shown that it slows aging in people.

research.text: The human evidence for rapamycin and aging is a few small randomized trials of safety, body composition, fitness and skin, lasting 8 weeks to 48 weeks. None measured how long people live or how fast they age clinically. The lifespan results come from mice.
Each is listed below as it was run.
Trials in older and middle-aged adults

research.title: Low-dose weekly rapamycin for 48 weeks (PEARL), 2025

facts.v: Decentralized, double-blind, placebo-controlled. Run by AgelessRx, whose staff wrote the paper and hold shares. The rapamycin was compounded.
Healthy adults aged 50 to 85, per the registry; 129 enrolled
48 weeks: placebo, 5 mg or 10 mg rapamycin once a week
Belly (visceral) fat by DXA scan (main outcome); blood tests; lean mass; bone; health surveys; side effects

research.found: Visceral fat did not change. Blood tests stayed in normal ranges. Adverse events were similar across groups. Lean mass and self-reported pain improved in women on 10 mg; some well-being scores improved on 5 mg. No other differences were found. The registry lists no posted results.

research.title: Weekly sirolimus with home exercise (RAPA-EX-01), 2026

facts.v: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled; registered as ACTRN12624000790549
13 weeks: 6 mg sirolimus or placebo once a week, plus a home strength and cycling program
Chair-stand repetitions (main outcome), grip, 6-minute walk, quality of life, blood markers, epigenetic age, side effects

research.found: Both groups improved. Sirolimus did not add to the gains. In the main analysis the difference was -2.13 repetitions in favor of placebo, not significant; two backup analyses favored placebo significantly. There were more adverse events on sirolimus (99 vs 63), including one serious pneumonia possibly linked to the drug.

src.label: Stanfield et al., J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle, 2026 (RAPA-EX-01)

research.title: Daily low-dose rapamycin in adults aged 70 to 95, 2018

facts.v: Randomized, placebo-controlled pilot, University of Texas Health Science Center, San Antonio
25 generally healthy older adults analyzed (11 rapamycin, 14 placebo); mean age 80.5
At least 8 weeks of 1 mg a day or placebo
Blood counts and chemistry, glucose tolerance, thinking tests, grip and walking, immune cells

research.found: No change in thinking, physical tests or glucose handling. Several red blood cell measures, including hemoglobin, fell on rapamycin. Side effects on rapamycin were facial rash, mouth sores and stomach upset.

research.title: Rapamycin cream on aging skin, 2019

facts.v: Exploratory, placebo-controlled, Drexel University dermatology clinic
36 adults over 40 with sun-damaged skin enrolled; 19 stopped or were lost to follow-up
Not stated in the abstract; the registry lists Sep to Nov 2017
Skin biopsy markers of cell aging (p16) and collagen; skin appearance

research.found: p16 fell and collagen VII rose in treated skin. The authors reported better skin appearance in several people. This was a topical cream, not a pill.

research.text: ClinicalTrials.gov lists more aging trials of sirolimus, for example: NCT06727305 (Phase 1/2, UT Southwestern, adults 65 and older, recruiting), NCT05237687 (Phase 2, functional decline in adults 65 and older, recruiting) and NCT05836025 (Phase 2, Columbia University, ovarian aging in women, active). None has posted results.

In genetically mixed mice, rapamycin fed from 600 days of age raised lifespan, based on age at 90% mortality, by 14% in females and 9% in males. A separate group started at 270 days also lived longer. These results have not been shown in people.

us.text: Sirolimus is FDA approved, by prescription, as Rapamune (1999), Fyarro (2021) and Hyftor (2022), and as generic tablets and oral solution. None is approved for aging or longevity. That use is off-label. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: oral solution approved September 15, 1999 (NDA 021083); tablets approved August 25, 2000 (NDA 021110). The label lists two uses: preventing kidney transplant rejection in people 13 and older, and treating LAM.
sirolimus protein-bound particles given by vein, approved November 22, 2021 (NDA 213312), for adults with an advanced or spreading tumor called malignant PEComa.
sirolimus gel for the skin, approved March 22, 2022 (NDA 213478), for facial angiofibroma in tuberous sclerosis, in adults and children 6 and older.
FDA's data list several generic sirolimus tablets and oral solutions approved under abbreviated applications.

the oral label warns of immune suppression, with higher risk of infection, lymphoma and other cancers. It says use in liver or lung transplant patients is not advised, because of excess deaths, graft loss and blood clots in the liver artery, and breakdown of airway joins after lung transplant.
using sirolimus to slow aging or for longevity is off-label. The PEARL trial used compounded rapamycin.

us.text: Compounded drugs are not FDA approved. FDA does not verify their safety, effectiveness or quality before they are marketed.

src.label: FDA, Compounding and the FDA: Q&A

us.text: FDA approval covers transplant, LAM, PEComa and a skin condition in tuberous sclerosis. It does not cover aging.

world.lead: Sirolimus is an approved prescription medicine in the US, the EU, the UK and Canada, and prescription-only in Australia. No regulator we checked has approved it for aging. It is not named on the WADA list.

countries.status: Approved medicine (Rapamune 1999; Fyarro 2021; Hyftor 2022; generics). Prescription-only. Longevity use is off-label.
Rapamune oral solution and tablets are marketed prescription drugs (first marketed 2001). Not approved for aging.

after.title: Sport
after.text: Sirolimus (rapamycin) is not named on the 2026 WADA Prohibited List or on the 2027 list, and neither list mentions mTOR inhibitors. Because it is an approved medicine, the list's S0 class for non-approved substances does not apply to it.

side.text: Sirolimus has a boxed warning for immune suppression, infection, lymphoma and other cancers. It can cause mouth sores, high blood fats, swelling, slow wound healing, lung inflammation and kidney protein loss. It can lower sperm counts. In older adults in aging trials, side effects were mostly minor, but the trials were small and short.

items.text: higher risk of infection and of lymphoma and other cancers, especially of the skin, from immune suppression. Not advised in liver or lung transplant patients.

the label warns that azoospermia (no sperm) or oligospermia (low sperm) may occur. Azoospermia has been reversible after stopping in most cases. In male rats, it shrank the testes and lowered sperm counts.
ovarian cysts and missed or heavy periods have been reported. It can harm an unborn baby; the label advises highly reliable birth control during use and for 12 weeks after.
swelling, high triglycerides and cholesterol, high blood pressure, raised creatinine, stomach pain, diarrhea, headache, fever, urinary infection, anemia, nausea, joint pain and low platelets.
items.lead: Common in transplant patients (30% or more):

items.text: mouth sores, diarrhea, stomach pain, nausea, colds, acne, chest pain, swelling, headache, dizziness, muscle pain and high cholesterol.
items.lead: Common in LAM patients (20% or more):

items.text: allergic reactions including angioedema, fluid build-up and poor wound healing, lung inflammation (some fatal), protein in the urine, reactivated viral infections, skin cancer, and avoiding live vaccines.

mouth sores, facial rash and stomach upset in a 25-person pilot, with small drops in red blood cell measures; more adverse events than placebo and one serious pneumonia in a 40-person trial; similar adverse events to placebo in PEARL.

src.label: Stanfield et al., J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle, 2026 (RAPA-EX-01)

items.text: mouth sores in 79% of people in its trial, plus tiredness, rash, infection, nausea and swelling; the label also warns of male infertility.

unconfirmed: We could not find Pfizer's own Rapamune label on DailyMed; the label cited is the version filed under the Rapamune tablet application (NDA 021110) by Mylan.
Drugs@FDA web pages did not load; approval dates come from FDA's openFDA data.
The PEARL paper's abstract does not give how many people finished; 129 enrolled per ClinicalTrials.gov.
We could not reach the TGA's ARTG register to list approved sirolimus products in Australia; only the Schedule 4 listing is confirmed.
The UK status rests on an MHRA safety update; we could not open the MHRA product database, which loads by script.
surprises: Rapamycin is widely discussed as a longevity drug, but the longest placebo-controlled aging trial we found (PEARL, 48 weeks) found no change in its main outcome, visceral fat.
In a 2026 trial in adults 65 to 85, weekly sirolimus did not add to exercise gains and may have reduced them, with more adverse events than placebo.
The sirolimus label warns that it can cause azoospermia (no sperm); none of the aging trials we read reported sperm counts.
